transcript:
Header: 2026-02-18 10:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya, Raj (Redwood) / Liam, Priya, Sara (Respira)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — still good on time?
[00:05] Liam O'Connor: Yep, go ahead.
[00:07] Maya Chen: Cool. So today's agenda: follow up on the throughput numbers we ran last week, dig into batching and queueing, and agree next steps for the canary. Raj, you ran a couple of benches — can you summarize?
[00:18] Raj Patel: Sure. Uh, we re-ran the mixed workload benchmark you sent — 20k requests over 30 minutes, sequence lengths from 32 to 512 tokens. Baseline was on our shared hosted pool using the mid-quant model. We saw average throughput about 360 tokens/sec per GPU, p50 latencies around 120ms per request, p95 around 820ms. We did notice lots of small batches — like 1 to 4 requests — which killed GPU efficiency.
[00:44] Priya Singh: Hmm that p95 is a bit higher than we expected. Our internal SLA is 600ms p95 for the endpoint in prod.
[00:51] Raj Patel: Right, and that aligns — the high p95 seems driven by head-of-line blocking where long seq requests prevent smaller ones getting served in the same micro-batch. Continuous batching with a smarter queueing policy should help.
[01:05] Sara Morales: Can you unpack continuous batching vs our current setup in plain terms?
[01:09] Raj Patel: Yeah — current approach basically flushes batches on a small timer or when batch size hits X. Continuous batching is the runtime keeping a rolling window, grouping requests by eligible sequence length and pad cost, and running kernels more frequently but with better packing. In practice that reduces the number of single-request kernels and improves GPU utilization. There's also prefix/KV cache reuse for chat sessions — that helps when you have repeated context.
[01:35] Liam O'Connor: We do have a lot of short-turn prompt traffic and then occasional long generative ones. So mixing hurts.
[01:41] Raj Patel: Exactly. Two quick levers: 1) set concurrency target — how many parallel streams we run to fill the GPU; 2) queueing policy — either strict FIFO (head-of-line) or fairness-based (we can let small fast requests jump ahead).
[01:56] Priya Singh: Are there tradeoffs to letting small requests jump ahead? We worry about starving long jobs.
[02:01] Raj Patel: Good point. We can implement token-budget fairness: short requests get prioritized up to a limit, and long jobs get burst slots so they don't wait forever. Also dynamic batching windows — e.g., 10ms soft window, 50ms hard cap — reduce latency without sacrificing throughput.
[02:19] Maya Chen: From the numbers we saw, if we push concurrency up to ~64 concurrent streams across the Dedicated pool we expect throughput to go up significantly, but you need to watch OOM and tail latencies. Raj, did you try a 64x run?
[02:33] Raj Patel: Not yet on the Dedicated pool — only on shared. I simulated concurrency up to 48, which bumped tokens/sec about 1.8x but p95 also tightened somewhat; however we didn't hit ideal batching because of the mixed seqs. A real Dedicated run at 64 will give better signals.
[02:48] Liam O'Connor: Ok, what does dedicated sizing look like? If we move to Dedicated, what's the minimal footprint to hit our 600ms p95 and target of 1.2M tokens/hour?
[02:58] Raj Patel: Quick ballpark — with continuous batching and kv-cache for sessions, maybe 4 GPUs (A100/80GB equivalence) with the optimized kernel selection. But that's a rough estimate; we should run a canary to validate. Also you can set autoscale burst to handle spikes without full reserved commit.
[03:15] Priya Singh: We need security and compliance info as well — SSO, audit logs, KMS.
[03:19] Maya Chen: We'll attach the security pack. For Dedicated or Private, KMS and audit log integration are supported; we'll include the SOC2 summary and the ops runbook.
[03:27] Sara Morales: Back to tuning — you mentioned queueing policy examples. Can you show recommended settings?
[03:32] Raj Patel: Sure I'll paste the doc after the call but high-level: concurrency target 48-64 (depending on GPU size), soft batching window 8-12ms, hard flush 50ms, token-based fairness with max short-jump of 80 tokens. Also enable prefix cache for chat session IDs to reduce cost on repeated context.
[03:51] Liam O'Connor: If we implement token-based fairness, is that in the hosted runtime today?
[03:56] Raj Patel: Yes, we've shipped a fairness queue in the runtime — it's on by default for Dedicated and can be toggled in Hosted per route. We'll provide sample config.
[04:05] Sara Morales: Any changes needed to our client side? We use a multithreaded request pool from the app.
[04:11] Raj Patel: Minimal — keep parallel streams and don't artificially serialize. If you can send concurrent short requests instead of batching them client-side into big single requests, the runtime can do packing more efficiently. We'll share best-practices.
[04:23] Maya Chen: Let's review the bench results Raj brought — can you walk us through the CSV highlights?
[04:27] Raj Patel: Yep. Row sample: concurrency=16 -> tokens/sec 340, p95 920ms. concurrency=32 -> tokens/sec 580, p95 760ms. concurrency=48 -> tokens/sec 630, p95 710ms. The inefficiency at lower conc is mainly due to many single-request kernels; at 48 we see better packing but still some long tails from the 512-token requests that block micro-batches.
[04:54] Priya Singh: So pushing concurrency helped but didn't eliminate p95 tail.
[04:58] Raj Patel: Correct — that's where queueing and fairness help. Also quantization profile matters; for instance integer-quant run reduced tokens/sec slightly but stable p95. We recommended the float16 quant profile for latency-critical endpoints.
[05:12] Liam O'Connor: We need concrete next bench to feel confident — what do you want from us?
[05:16] Raj Patel: If you can share one hour of traffic, we can replay it against a Dedicated test pool and try the following runs: baseline, concurrency=64 with fairness on, concurrency=64 with fairness off, and concurrency=32 with continuous batching tuned. That should show impact.
[05:32] Sara Morales: We can extract the sample — we'll get it today.
[05:35] Priya Singh: Timeline for results?
[05:37] Raj Patel: We'll aim to run the burst (1 hour replay compressed into 10-15 mins) and return a CSV + dashboard within 48 hours. So target Monday/Tuesday.
[05:46] Maya Chen: Great. Also pricing note — moving to Dedicated changes unit economics. I'll send a short pricing table comparing hosted vs dedicated for the targeted throughput including autoscale burst costs.
[05:57] Liam O'Connor: On fallback policies — if Dedicated is saturated can we failover to hosted variants?
[06:03] Raj Patel: Yes, smart routing supports fallback to compatible model variants in hosted region. You can define policy: only fallback for non-sensitive traffic or for X% of requests. We'll include routing policy examples.
[06:15] Priya Singh: Any immediate risks we should be watching during canary?
[06:19] Raj Patel: Tail latency spikes if clients push huge concurrent long sequences; OOM if concurrency is too high for the model memory footprint; and KV cache thrash if session IDs aren't sticky. We'll set monitoring thresholds and alert hooks.
[06:32] Sara Morales: Sounds good. Let's confirm the action items.
[06:35] Maya Chen: Raj to run burst bench at 64 and share CSV by Friday, Liam to share traffic sample by tomorrow, Maya to send pricing and security docs. Schedule tentative canary next week.
[06:48] Liam O'Connor: Confirmed. One quick Q — do you recommend we change our client timeouts? Currently it's 10s.
[06:54] Raj Patel: For interactive flows, 10s is fine, but if you push longer generative jobs, bump to 30s and rely on streaming so frontends don't block. Use server-sent events for progress updates.
[07:06] Priya Singh: Noted.
[07:08] Maya Chen: Anything else?
[07:10] Sara Morales: No, that's all. Thanks everyone.
[07:12] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

Summary / Closing (approx): recap of bench numbers, plan to run 64-concurrency burst, share configs for continuous batching and fairness queueing, provide pricing/security pack, and schedule canary.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attributions and minor word swap errors (e.g., "kv cache" transcribed as "k-v cash" in some spots).
